newsitem.title: POLAND: Rain on mourning Poland threatens new floods.
newsitem.headline: Rain on mourning Poland threatens new floods.

text.p: Poland's official crisis committee said renewed floods were on the way after rain fell throughout Friday on the western third of a country already mourning 48 deaths in a two-week calamity.
"The rain has been falling since morning over effectively one third of Poland from Koszalin (in the north) down to the southern border," committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said.
"We must expect there will be a new flood in those same regions where it happened before," Pomes told Reuters, adding that it was hard to say on what scale it would be.
"As for the effects, we will see in the next hours," said Pomes from the committee set up to deal with the disaster.
He said the rain was lighter than downpours two weeks ago which unleashed the region's worst natural disaster in centuries, but the ground was soaked and reservoirs full.
For hundreds of thousands of exhausted residents of almost a thousand towns and villages hit by the earlier floods, the rain promised the return of a nightmare.
But Pomes said this time Poles were better prepared with evacuation plans and flood defences.
In the past two weeks, the floods swamped more than 4,000 sq km of Poland, leaving a shroud of filth and the danger of disease in its wake.
They inundated the south and then sent great swells northwards along the Wisla and Odra rivers, submerging the city streets of Wroclaw and Opole in the southwest.
On Friday, flags were at half mast, churches held services and public broadcasters played serious music to mark a day of mourning.

Parliament during the night passed more than 20 bills allowing the government to increase borrowing and to rush both funds and aid to smitten areas. In the early hours, President Aleksander Kwasniewski announced he had signed them into law.
Parliament also hastily amended the communist-era state of emergency law, cutting its most undemocratic provisions, so it could be applied in case of a new round of the calamity.

Kwasniewski supported the prime minister in opposing opposition calls to declare a state of emergency now in hard-hit regions, arguing that this would delay September 21 parliamentary elections and was unnecessary.

"But if it turns out that tomorrow or the next day we are dealing with a serious threat to very many provinces of Poland, we will have no alternative, we will have to take the decision," Kwasniewski said.

Poland's central bank rushed to the aid of the zloty, repeatedly selling dollars as speculators drove the Polish currency lower and investors pulled out amid fears that flood relief measures would harm Poland's finances.
The bank's defence proved effective and the zloty closed slightly higher against a basket of foreign currencies.
In the neighbouring Czech Republic, where at least 45 people have died, foreboding gripped the country after forecasters also predicted heavy rain.
